items.body:
Absolutely filthy/screwed club gunk  and no-wave machine music from Murray Collier (Grim Lusk, Dip Friso) & Conal Blake (Feedback Moves, Domestic Exile), working together as Inweys and highly tipped FFO Actress, MMM, Wino, V/Vm's 'Machine Component' series...

“Inweys debut release arrives as four pieces of broken body music. Lurking, barely human fragments brought into the present. Using a short drum-machine improvisation as core material, the pieces are formed from a processes of mining and re-mining for small details, with each fragment zoomed in on and turned into new pieces. There’s a transformation taking place, but one that doesn’t obscure the materiality of the recording tapes as sticky, corrosive matter. On skewed and stretched fabric they enact their palimpsestic play, sketching and altering the grid with itchy technologies. What their edits and improvisations don’t say they let space say the rest, with vacuum aerated frames for bass to diffuse and beats to wriggle. More King Tubby than Cage, more Mantronix than Reich: minimalism with molten tips.

Both Conal and Murray’s past work has embraced malleable and iterative technologies; music whose feeliness figures itself out in space in a messy precomposed/improvised dialectic. This is the sort of thing most “new music” experimentalists (or anyone who spends most of their time obsessively manipulating tapes in expensive studios) often can’t achieve; a liveness, birthed from learning in situated play. Like the lore of Phuture’s Acid Trax, a poverty of material is at the heart of this, rendering the work with an abortive conviction: a corpse waking to consciousness becomes amphibious. Instead of the composer we have a relation, two people navigating the awkward spooling between the two reels of tape. Inweys is scots for “inwards”, and in their working process this is what they do. But the result is circular motion. Until the tape runs out, all in ways move out”. "

Fielding Hope.
items._genre: experimental electronic / no-wave / club music / tape manipulation
items._cn_summary: Inweys的首张专辑由Murray Collier与Conal Blake合作，以一台鼓机的即兴录音为核心素材，通过反复挖掘、放大、重组其中的微小碎片，构建出四首破碎的俱乐部声响。整体手法强调材料的物质性与腐蚀感，磁带被拉伸、扭曲、叠层，留下粘稠而粗糙的质地。作品拒绝追求干净的结构，而是让留白与真空般的低频空间成为节奏的延伸，呈现出介于King Tubby与John Cage之间、混合Mantronix与Steve Reich的融化式极简主义。两位音乐家将即兴与预构置于辩证关系中，借助磁带两轮之间的尴尬缠绕，以关系的姿态取代作曲者的权威，贫乏的素材反而赋予作品一种决绝的说服力。整张专辑走向内向，却在结果上形成回环运动，直至磁带走完。

items.body:
Alex Zhang Hungtai pivots yet again on 'Orion/Mother', playing (mostly) trumpet alongside some of the New York City underground scene's most intriguing improvisers, including Kwami Winfield, Laura Cocks, Lester St. Louis, TAK Ensemble's Madison Greenstone, 75 Dollar Bill's Che Chen and Leo Chang.

 'Orion/Mother' has its roots in a set of home recordings Zhang made with some of his talented local friends; "playing with you all deeply informed my current understanding in improvisation," he explains in his thank you note, "without you this album would not have existed." So over a two week period, in a rehearsal space in New York, he invited a handful of his friends to start "an ad-hoc group", playing trumpet over chopped up home recordings and wrenching them into the future. And while the finished article - split into two distinct sections - is long, it's fully worthy of your attention. As always, Zhang brings a unique ear into the room, resisting any usual improv tropes to concentrate on sounds that most artists would avoid - unruly resonances, glitches, off-piste rhythms and unsubtle interferences.

At it's best, the record sounds like jazz specters vanishing thru faded noise remnants and the wreckage of lost experiments. On 'Shadow Integration', Zhang's brassy wails echo out over a slippery, semi-rhythmic drum machine pattern, and on 'Tanhäuser Gate', the trumpet is even more isolated, weeping over a muted soundscape that's credited simply as "Ableton" on the accompanying notes. He maintains the same energy when he's working side-by-side with his collaborators, too, finding space for Winfield's circuit bent belches on 'Nataraja' and Chen and Chang's percussion on the jaw-droppingly spannered opener 'Sidewinder'. And even when the tone shifts on 'Mother', heading into a lighter (comparatively at least) zone on the woodwind-heavy 'Kali', Zhang has a knack for tying everything together with his lyrical performance. Just peep the title track, almost seven minutes of uncanny clanks and Tōru Takemitsu-strength murmurs that Zhang butters with pure improvised emotion.
items._genre: free improvisation / experimental jazz / electronic / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以小号为核心，召集纽约地下即兴圈的乐手，在两周内围绕张的居家录音碎片展开即兴对话。制作上刻意回避传统即兴套路，专注于失控的共鸣、失真的节拍与粗糙的干扰声，将小号置于鼓机、断路器改装设备与静音音景之间。小号时而孤鸣于电子残骸之上，时而与打击乐形成棱角分明的碰撞，末段转向木管主导的轻盈质地。专辑以纯即兴情绪串联松散的声响碎片，整体呈现出实验爵士与电子即兴的深度交融。

items.body:
Adrian Rew's properly hypnotic cult classic 'Slot Machine Music' has finally been reissued and it sounds even more terrifying and prescient than it did back in 2013 at the height of the basement noise era. One of the best environmental recording records bar none - don't sleep.

Back in 2009, PAN released its fourth album, 'Kenrimono', a set of recordings made by Greek sound artist Ilios at Japanese pachinko halls. The sheer density of it was as shocking and as intense as anything the noise genre had to offer, packed out with whirring, crunching and chiming resonances that took you to the smokey epicenter of the Japanese gambling world. And when 'Slot Machine Music' arrived a few short years later we assumed the sound would be similar; we were wrong. Initially dropped via Rew's own Ergot Records on CDr before the great Aaron Dilloway stepped in to handle the vinyl edition on his own Hanson imprint, the album seemingly grew from the Midwestern noise petri dish - but it wasn't an exercise in aesthetic posturing, using the racket of the modern American casino to mimic the intensity of a Wolf Eyes set. Instead, Rew was drawn to the experience itself, that's been meticulously designed by malign forces to guide behavior: those trapped inside the casino's four walls are seduced into spending more, losing more and returning to do it all over again.

Rew didn't know much about the environment when he visited Cleveland's Horseshoe Casino for the first time in 2013 armed with an Olympus LS-11 recorder and a camera. And over four months, he developed a peculiar relationship with the culture, surreptitiously taping the soundscapes at various Midwestern locations - in Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois - while attempting not to lose too much cash in the process. And it's a warts-n-all set, with dialog snippets and outdoor ambiance giving us more than simply the dense mass of chimes and stings and themes that you'd hear on the casino floor itself. What Rew is able to do is create a snapshot of a time and place, capturing the sheer desolation of the casino experience and using it to drive a narrative that Robert Altman would be proud of. The first thing you notice is that each machine's sounds are in tune with the next; "game designers," explains Rew, "tune their machines to the key of C in order to optimize harmonic cohesion." So although Rew's recordings are full-bodied, they're never too chaotic or discordant. 

Indeed, if you check in for the entire record - 2013's iconic 'Slot Machine Music' and its 2014 sequel 'Slot Machine Music Vol. 2' - you'll be lulled into the same false sense of security that entrances casino regulars. It's almost like ambient music, packed out with tiny sonic details that some well-paid sound engineer-cum-neurologist worked for years to figure out. Guided meditation music? New age crypto-psychedelia? It's all here, packaged in neon-lit one-armed-bandits aimed to target the dopamine centers of aging boomers with money to burn. And the best thing about the recordings is that Rew keeps some of the chatter intact, so we can hear him tangling with casino security, or haggling with his slot machine neighbors over change. We can hear the cheers and claps as paltry sums are won while vast fortunes are lost. The best moment for us comes when Rew wanders outside Grand Victoria Casino in Elgin, Illinois at the dead of night, the crickets singing as the machines echo from behind grand double doors. A freight train rushes past and blots out any other sound, distorting the recording.

It's a good reminder that although you might be able to hide from reality inside the casino, the Midwest will inevitably confront you with its rusted truth.
items._genre: field recording / sound art / noise / experimental / ambient
items._cn_summary: Adrian Rew的《Slot Machine Music》系列是一组以美国中西部赌场为对象的田野录音作品。录音跨越密歇根、印第安纳、俄亥俄、伊利诺伊等多地，使用Olympus LS-11便携录音机在Horseshoe Casino等地持续采集数月。录音不仅包含老虎机自身的嗡鸣、撞击与清脆响声，还保留了环境对话与户外声响，呈现赌场这一经过精密设计、旨在操控行为的声学空间。Rew发现所有机器被统一调至C大调以追求和声上的统一感，使得整张专辑虽层次密集却并不失序，介于环境音乐与冥想音景之间。评论将其置于噪音与声音艺术脉络中，与PAN厂牌发行的Ilios的《Kenrimono》并列讨论，强调其作为环境录音杰作的独特地位。

items._cn_summary: 这是Mixed Band Philanthropist在1987年发行的专辑《The Impossible Humane》，由德国独立厂牌Selektion以限量300张、手绘封面形式发行。作品汇集了来自英国、法国、德国、比利时、意大利、瑞典、美国、加拿大及日本等地三十余位实验音乐人和噪音艺术家的原始磁带素材，经主创人员剪辑、拼贴、混音及母带处理而成。专辑横跨噪音、工业、具体音乐、磁带拼贴、声音艺术与极简主义等多个领域，将Organum、Merzbow、Nurse With Wound、Asmus Tietchens、P16.D4等团体的素材重新编织为连贯的听觉叙事。这种跨越国界的素材采集与拼贴手法，将工业音乐的反叛精神与具体音乐的解构逻辑融为一体。

items.body:
reMASTERed edition of all 5 voulmes of Carsten Nicolai aka Alva Noto’s classic Xerrox series - exploring what happens when copies are made of copies of copies of copies etc..... a beautiful way to parse affective signals from noise and a big RIYL Ryuichi Sakamoto, Fennesz, Romance.

‘Xerrox’ marked a pivotal juncture of Alva Noto’s process-based, multimedia art, when it transformed from precision-tooled, pulsating minimalism to diffuse states of cinematic atmosphere. By the point of the first volume's release, Carsten Nicolai had spent over a decade rising to acclaim for his exquisite, minimalist glitch works, including contemporary classics in duo with Ryuichi Sakamoto. 

But ‘Xerrox’ would radically alter his work’s aesthetic away from microscopic, pointillist grammar to explorations of lusher textural and widescreen fascinations, systematically sampling and displacing familiar, everyday sounds - advert jingles, phone “hold” tones, film scores - within swelling symphonic structures that exist in paradoxical states of glacial stasis and noisy chaos, synthetic and organic, arguably sowing seeds for his work accompanying the lavish cinematography of ‘The Revenant’ years later.

The albums still hold an uncannily nostalgic pull over anyone who was there at the time, as Nicolai appeared to draw from his collaborator Sakamoto’s feel for misty-eyed melancholy across the set, resulting in pieces that feel like peak Fennesz in ‘Haloid Xerrox Copy 111’, or surely resemble pre-echoes of Romance’s swooning silhouettes in ‘Haloid Xerrox Copy 3 (Paris)’, or Michael Mann-esque modern city panoramas in ‘Haloid v Copy 11’, thru the Kevin Drumm-meets-John Carpenter tension of ‘Haloid Xerrox Copy 9’.
items._genre: glitch / ambient / experimental electronic / microsound / cinematic
items._cn_summary: Xerrox系列五卷再版合集，探讨复制再复制所产生的声音偏移与情感残留。Alva Noto以日常声音为素材——广告旋律、电话等待音、电影配乐——将其采样、位移、重组，融入庞大对称的交响化结构中，在冰川般的静止与噪音混沌之间形成张力。音乐语汇从早期精密的极简故障脉冲，转向更宽阔的质地探索，呈现烟雾般的怀旧氛围，类似Fennesz的朦胧光泽或Carpenter式的悬疑张力。这一转变也为其日后为《荒野猎人》创作电影配乐埋下伏笔，将微观声响语法拓展为电影化的大银幕叙事，与Sakamoto合作中的忧郁气质在此系列中被独立放大，成为处理信号与噪音关系的一种美学范式。

items.body:
The second ever public performance by Nurse With Wound, captured on tape in 1984 and held in Steven Stapleton's archive across the four decades since, now available on a vinyl edition for the first time - every copy painted by hand, edition of 300.

You get the measure of this one with Steven Stapleton’s assertion that this was less a gig and more a “series of confrontations with audiences who often had no idea what they were watching.” which is basically everything we hope for watching pretty much anything.

It belongs to a moment when Stapleton, working alongside collaborators including David Tibet, Andrew McKenzie of The Hafler Trio, and a rotating cast of percussionists and string players, was carrying NWW briefly out of the studio. The performance moves through the territory NWW had been mapping across Homotopy to Marie and Nature Unveiled: long passages of pre-recorded tape collage assembled by Stapleton and McKenzie, ridden over by live electronics, voice, percussion, and a surreal theatrical instinct.

or as the band call it, “a collective groping”

aye.
items._genre: experimental / industrial / tape collage / live electronics / avant-garde
items._cn_summary: 这是Nurse With Wound乐队1984年的一次现场演出录音，尘封四十年后首次以黑胶形式发行，每张均由手工绘制，限量300张。演出由Steven Stapleton与David Tibet、Hafler Trio的Andrew McKenzie及多位打击乐与弦乐乐手合作完成。内容以预录磁带拼贴为基底，叠加现场电子、人声、打击乐与超现实剧场化表演，延续了乐队在《Homotopy to Marie》与《Nature Unveiled》时期的声音探索。Stapleton本人将这次演出描述为"与观众的连续对峙"，乐队则称之为"集体摸索"。整场演出介于音乐、噪音与行为艺术之间，呈现出强烈的不可预测性与挑衅性，是Nurse With Wound罕见的公开演出文献。

items.body:
Taking their cues from the 1968 silent film 'Le Révélateur', Berlin-based Hungarian-Transylvanian artist Réka Csiszér (aka VÍS) and Radwan Ghazi Moumneh (aka Jerusalem in My Heart) use synths, voices and various instruments to breathe new life into Philippe Garrel’s iconic work.

If you heard last year's grimly romantic 'Danse des Larmes', Csiszér's second VÍS album and another one-of-a-kind oddity on the always good Heat Crimes label, you might already have an inkling of how good this one's gonna be. The record was made between November 2025 and February of this year between Zurich and Montréal, where Moumneh runs the legendary Hotel2Tango studio, and it's some of the most chilling material we've heard from either artist. The duo first met in 2018 and initially debuted their soundtrack to 'Le Révélateur' live in 2023; the film had been a long-time favorite of Moumneh's, but Csiszér didn't need much convincing - its themes of displacement and disorientation made immediate sense to an artist who'd grown up with an ever-shifting idea of home, born in East Germany before moving to Vienna.

And after performing their free-flowing soundtrack a handful of times, improvising within a set of tight themes, they decided to document the project properly, borrowing a mate's house in Montréal for a few weeks to record the meat and bones. And although the baseline for the album version of the collaboration is the same ("composed through improvisation," they say), it sounds as if the themes have been weathered and lived in a little at this stage. If you've seen the film, you'll realize it's the unique mood - accentuated by Garrel's stark lighting and Michel Fournier's bold black-and-white cinematography - that carries it, and it's this high-contrast, peripatetic motion that Csiszér and Moumneh capture so magically. 

Opening track 'wahid – واحد' suggests darkness ahead with its eerie environmental sounds (creaking gates, crackly vinyl, caged birds), scraped strings and isolated synths that accompany a shot of a couple smoking in a door frame, their silhouettes cut out of the sunlight. But like the film itself, it's the juxtaposition that makes it hit; 'ithnan – اثنان' is almost celestial, an uncanny hymn made from analogue drones and soft-focus wordless voices. And when they shift into grittier territory on 'arba'a – أربعة', a short distorted instrumental that sits alongside a shot of a young boy seemingly torturing a doll, the album's long centerpiece 'khamsa – خمسة' follows it up with Csiszér's most stunning vocal performance, that lifts a long shot of the nomadic family walking down a forest road.

It's minimal but never for dull for even a moment - best viewed alongside Garrel's film for the optimum experience.
items._genre: experimental / sound collage / drone / ambient / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这是一张为菲利普·加雷尔1968年无声电影《Le Révélateur》创作的原声专辑，由柏林匈牙利裔特兰西瓦尼亚艺术家Réka Csiszér（VÍS）与黎巴嫩裔音乐人Radwan Ghazi Moumneh（Jerusalem in My Heart）在苏黎世与蒙特利尔的Hotel2Tango工作室合作完成。两位艺术家以即兴为基底，在合成器、人声与多样乐器间构建出与影片高对比黑白影像相呼应的声景。开场曲以吱嘎作响的门声、唱片噪点与笼中鸟鸣营造不安氛围，其后模拟合成器长音与无词人声形成近乎神圣的吟唱，扭曲失真片段穿插于影片的压抑画面之间。整张作品极简却始终保持张力，环境声响与器乐即兴交织，被评价为两位艺术家迄今最具寒意的创作。乐评建议与原片同步观看以获得完整体验。

items.body: When their latest album Smash and Grab came out, I cheekily claimed Ballister might be the best band in the world. I still stand by that statement, and what could be more fitting for Dave Rempis and his Aerophonic label than to celebrate their 50th physical release with a new recording by that outfit? The only question that came up beforehand possibly was what to do to make it special? The answer was relatively simple: You bring in a real powerhouse to give the whole thing even more momentum. And what could be more natural than inviting a bassist for that? Luke Stewart (of Irreversible Entanglements fame) was practically the obvious choice. However, that also means that the expectations for a recording like this are incredibly high. For Clocking the Wheel Ballister could have done what we all love them for: simply mixing up their famous cocktail of high energy music, speed metal, free jazz, and brutalistic power, slap it right in our faces, and everyone would have been happy. And of course they do deliver this mix - but they also present another side. Especially in the first part of this double CD, “Carpet Joint,” Dave Rempis (as always on different saxes) and Fred Lonberg-Holm (cello) trade off so effortlessly for three minutes that you’d think you were at a chamber concert. What is more, they leave room for solos, for example for percussionist Paal Nilssen-Love, who presents rhythms with a Latin American flavor, laying the groundwork for two ballad-like interludes - something we’re not used to hearing too often from the band. However, you immediately find yourself wishing they would do that every now and then. The icing on the cake is an almost Evan-Parker-esque solo by Rempis and a one-minute nod by the band to themselves, to one of their catchiest riffs (if such a thing even exists in this kind of music). In this piece, which the band performs as a trio, we are once again reminded of what makes Ballister so unique: it’s the combination of these very different styles and sounds, the way the dynamics flow into one another, that they so effortlessly blend into a cohesive whole. Finally, Luke Stewart joins in on “Sauce for the Goose,” the second track that makes up the entirety of the second CD, and you’re faced with a changed band. For bassists, it’s not easy to keep up with Ballister - with the trio’s force, its radicalism, its rawness, its unvarnished authenticity. The band could literally run you over. But Stewart immediately immerses himself in Ballister’s sound, locking in with Nilssen-Love’s drumming to catapult the higher voices of the cello and saxophone forward. His driving energy is like a tightly stretched rubber band - elastic, yielding, flexible, but always with enough tensile strength to bounce back like a trampoline, as the liner notes put it. And Stewart is also given plenty of space to make his mark, whether in duo or solo passages. All in all “Sauce for the Goose” shows that there is still a lot of potential with the Ballister project. Stewart’s presence draws even more energy out of the other three members, giving rise to new sound combinations (the use of electronics shines through here and there and Dave Rempis, in particular, is almost reinventing himself) and dynamics. After twelve albums, Ballister is far from running out of ideas; the band still has plenty in store. For me, they’re still the best band in the world - at least when it comes to freely improvised music. Clocking the Wheel is available as a double CD and as a download. You can listen to “Sauce for the Goose“ on the Aerophonic bandcamp site, where you can also order the album: Clocking The Wheel by Ballister + Luke Stewart Email This BlogThis! items.body: Miserere Luminis – Sidera (Debemur Morti, Mar 6) Emerging from the ashes of Gris, Quebecois legends Icare and Neptune revived Miserere Luminis in 2023 with Ordalie, a record that proved the trio (the third is Annatar of Sombres Forêts) was much more than a mere side project. But this is their first true masterpiece, a triumphant showcase of technicality, songwriting, and emotion. For me, it’s usually less as more when it comes to black metal, but all of Sidera’s many layers are balanced in such a way that it avoids the common trappings: it’s cathartic but not histrionic, progressive but not indulgent. The pained howls spin scripture of existential woe, the sparing strings add aching harmonies, and the grooves lead upward into sublime oblivion. Negation – 2022_Q3 & 2022_Q4 (WAY, Mar 7) Though he’s been active for more than a decade at this point, you could fit all of Negation’s discography on a single CD with room to spare. Project mastermind Kieran Morris exhaustively sculpts and tweaks his sound experiments into laser-focused documents, as evidenced by concise releases like Solar Torque and 1988 Mitsubishi Montero Sport. The utilitarian materialism of 2022_Q3 & 2022_Q4‘s title extends to its contents, an assimilation of audio surplus generated by a bout of tedious desk labor and such prestigious programs as Microsoft Teams. Listening with speakers is a must; this is the NY phenom’s most complex and spatial work so far, exploding with dizzying technicality and building tension with well-placed downtime. Ruda Vera – Suc de Rocs (sedicions, March) One of a pair of new cassette releases on Catalonian hermit Ruda Vera’s own sedicions imprint, Suc de Rocs is a welcome reminder of what makes his art so special. In contrast to the short sketches of Anthimeria, this single-sided C90 collects lengthy meditations that are as humble and inscrutable as ever. Even more so than previous releases, it’s never quite clear where the sound sources end and the rattle and slur of the artist’s shambolic tape machines begin. Everything blends together in a single stream of dirt, glass, and ferric oxide. Ruda Vera’s music aligns with his collage work (see some examples in his new interview in Untitled) in how both fixate on singular masses of textures: the mash of motion in an everyday action, the crusty cacophony of closely recorded junk. Jack Sheen performed by Apartment House – Press (The Trilogy Tapes, Jan 22) If you’re at all familiar with my taste you know I’m not much of a classical head. There’s a certain kind of humanity I have to hear in music for it to resonate with me, and I don’t usually find it in formal composition. Jack Sheen’s work is one of a few notable exceptions. Press expands the haunting harmonics and elliptical arpeggios he explored with Solo for Cello to a quintet, with prolific British ensemble Apartment House embracing the unusual tunings and metal mutes required for this ambitious score. It’s spellbinding music, a diaphanous spiderweb that trembles on the edge of the abyss, faint grey light glinting on the dewy strands. Nu No – Canto Ventríloquo (La République des Granges, May 15) As I wrote in my review, Canto Ventríloquo reminded me to catch up on everything Nu No (Nuno Marques Pinto) has released since 2019’s Turva Lingua, so it gets props just for that. It’s also a testament to the quality of the tape that it stands out as a new high point for the Portuguese polymath even against such a consistent catalog. Each listen through is like opening an old grimy treasure chest, the contents of which you think you already know, only to be surprised every time. I’ve found myself growing to appreciate the more reserved cantos, wherein Pinto restricts himself to either only voice (“IX”) or no voice at all (“VII”)—the latter of which is an inflection point to close the A side, the winding tension like vocal cords priming for the next utterance. Slacking – Curling Pupils of Sleep ’Neath Bended Moon (Fusty, May 27) For those who have heard any of Jim Lerario’s recent material as Slacking—especially those who have witnessed it live—it comes as no surprise that Curling Pupils of Sleep ‘Neath Bended Moon is already sold out. The Pittsburgh wizard has steadily and mercilessly improved since his very first tape in 2019, and this first LP outing is the culmination of all of it. Magnetic tape is Lerario’s paintbrush, and on Sacred Heart of Reinvention and “Do What Thou Droop” from his split with Black Corolla he coated canvases with vivid nightmare hues. There’s a newfound fluidity on Curling Pupils, though. The shifting, slithering noise is as psychedelic as ever, but it’s also cathartic, even ecstatic at points (hear “Mean Bone”, which channels Dilloway’s “Eight Cut Scars”). Lucy Bedroque – B4C (self-released, May 10) To tide fans over until the promised but as-yet-unheard follow-up to last year’s Unmusique, C, extremely online MC and producer Lucy Bedroque (Jeremiah Mark) dropped the aptly titled B4C in May. A thrown-together collection of seven tracks, some of which may or may not be on the album, the EP has all the markings of a forgettable bonus release—that is, until it starts playing, and the magic makes itself known. “006 Finessaa” and “C Section” are some of Mark’s best songs yet, rawer and rougher takes on the young artist’s candy-coated approach to rage that capture their infectious live presence. I’m generally not huge on prettifun but his two features fit well here. There are some missteps, likely due to a rushed rollout (what the hell is that kick on “Bowser”), but the imperfections make it all the more perfect. Endlessly replayable. Temple Guard – Citadel in Flames (worldwide, Jun 11) Citadel in Flames snuck up on me. Lured by the killer cover art, I told myself I’d heard this same sound done to death and that Temple Guard wouldn’t make any more of a lasting impression than the countless other new heavy hardcore bands I’ve heard recently. But then “Blood Makes the Rain Fall” kicked in, and it slowly became clear that this five-piece stands apart from the horde. The bellowed lyrics range from doomsday resignation to militant eco-radicalism, sharpened with martial medieval imagery befitting of the visual aesthetic. The fury ramps to apocalyptic fervor with “The Weight of Undying Shame”, a crushing siege engine of a track fortified with the most evil breakdown of the year.

items.body: There is a future in which song arrives without any blood, sweat, or tears. No trembling hands, no bad decisions, no overloaded mixer, no cracked voice breaking at precisely the wrong and therefore perfect moment. Algorithms compose, mix, and master with surgical precision, polishing away all of art’s beautiful accidents until only cold machine efficiency remains. In the world imagined by Wie Ein Gott Records for its new compilation Made By Humans, that future has already won. Music creation has been automated almost completely, and human creators are no longer treated as contributors but as patterns of noise in the system. The final rupture comes when an entity known as CPK1310-5L receives a Nobel Prize for discovering God’s Formula: a set of harmonic ratios and progression templates capable of producing the “perfect” song across any known genre. Perfection, of course, is another word for death when nothing vulnerable or dangerous is allowed to live inside it. Against that sterile horizon, a counter-movement begins to flicker. These songs stutter, distort, sweat, bleed, and misbehave. They are transmitted through HUMDRM, an anti-DRM encryption system available only to biological listeners, unlocked by heartbeat verification and marked with a phrase that reads like a warning label and a promise: Made By Humans. The Berlin label gathers fourteen such transmissions here, assembling an international cross-section of contemporary underground artists working through industrial EBM, dark disco, rave, darkwave, synth-punk, and post-club experimentation. The result is less a conventional compilation than a dossier of sonic contraband: body music smuggled past the machines. And one of those MADE BY HUMAN transmissions is Brood Faye’s “I Could B U.” Los Angeles’ Brood Faye is the industrial darkwave/EBM project of Zach Webber, whose background in theatre and narration is mangled into a voice built for warehouse floors, dungeon rooms, and scorched circuitry. The project took form in 2021, welding analog synth pressure, horror-punk bite, industrial clang, and political disgust into songs that feel like dread and desire trying to occupy the same body. On “I Could B U,” that pressure turns strangely devotional. A pulsing techno beat and buzzing synths carry something like a Madchester-meets-industrial pagan-punk ritual, while Brood Faye’s breathy vocals snarl and growl in sparse flashes, withholding just enough language to make the body fill in the rest. The song is transcendent and dance-driven, a piece of body music that moves like a convulsion, a flirtation, and an arcane spell. Listen to Brood Faye’s “I Could B U” below: The compilation’s roster gives that human revolt its geography. San Francisco’s Pink Stiletto opens the set with “Ice Eyes,” bringing the project’s pink-and-sharp analogue synth attack into focus: 80s new wave, Italo disco, post-punk, and early EBM rendered with a bilingual glare and a glamorous edge that knows exactly how to cut. Los Angeles duo Sleek Teeth appear with “Powerless,” pulling moody dark electronics into a sleek pressure chamber of synthpop hooks, EBM pulse, and late-night dislocation. Their work has always understood the club as both refuge and trap: a place where isolation becomes rhythmic enough to survive. Germany’s Desolate Discotheque offers “Одиночество,” its Cyrillic title translating to loneliness, an apt word for a project connected to the Berlin cold-room circuit and the independent cassette and vinyl label Crave Tapes. Here, desolation does not mean emptiness. It means a room with one machine still blinking in the dark. Blood Handsome’s “Fear (Itself)” brings Gerren Reach’s cinematic Los Angeles darkwave into the compilation, placing retro synth glow inside a mood of romantic paranoia. Blood Handsome has long worked in that liminal zone where post-punk melancholy, nostalgic electronics, and noir atmosphere meet like strangers in a parking lot at 3 a.m. FUEDAL arrive with “Bought,” carrying their hard-tested EBM/industrial charge into the machine. The Los Angeles project thrives on tension: percussion like boots on concrete, synths like exposed wiring, and the faint smirk of masochism turning rage into release. Blood Rave’s “The Burning Field” pushes the compilation toward a scorched gothic dance floor, channeling Napa/Bay Area darkwave and EBM into something monolithic, pulsing, and doomed in exactly the right way. Abby Knives & Manuel Matarasso bring Buenos Aires intensity to the roster with “You Can Only Feel It.” Their contribution moves through EBM, industrial, and techno with a title that doubles as a thesis: some things cannot be optimized, translated, or explained. They have to pass through the body first. Dildox’s “Cortex” sends the nerve signals haywire. The Los Angeles duo smashes industrial, darkwave, and synth-pop into punk-body chaos, keeping the funk in the grind and the ritual in the sweat. Their music does not ask politely to be let in; it kicks the door down and starts rearranging the furniture. Healng’s “WHATS FUNNY” draws from Cincinnati heavy electronics, EBM-techno, industrial, and synth-punk, reducing humor to a threat whispered through machinery. It is body music with a clenched jaw, the sound of a laugh caught halfway between mockery and malfunction. Static Ghost keeps the pressure violent and physical with “Cut A Man’s Throat.” The Washington State EBM project pulls from industrial’s underbelly, dealing in muscular momentum, coldwave abrasion, synthetic control, and rhythms that feel less programmed than weaponized. Temptrix appears with “History Of Time (INHALT Remix),” where Texas darkwave and body music are pulled into a sleek nocturnal confession. Desire, gothic drama, and machine discipline circle each other under red light, each one pretending not to notice the other’s teeth. God Tongue’s “the end” drags Seattle’s Acid Body Wave/Acid Body Rave into the terminal corridor: EBM muscle, acid corrosion, minimal-wave chill, hardware grit, and a B-movie smirk. The duo’s work feels like somebody fed a warehouse PA after midnight and taught it to hallucinate. Finally, Leere Menge closes with “Halt Mich.” The Berlin darkwave duo of Aarnav from Permanent Daylight and Deborah from Clichée turns post-punk and darkwave into a softer but no less haunted exit: lush synth space, provocative percussion, and ethereal vocal ache lingering after the machines have gone quiet. Taken together, these fourteen tracks do not argue for human music by sounding clean. They argue by sounding alive: imperfect, body-locked, erotic, damaged, funny, volatile, and impossible to fully optimize. Made By Humans will be released via Wie Ein Gott Records on July 10, 2026. items._cn_summary: 这张合辑以反乌托邦叙事为框架，设定了一个音乐创作被算法全面接管的时代，人类的创作沦为系统中的噪声模式。柏林厂牌Wie Ein Gott汇集十四组国际地下艺术家，通过虚构的HUMDRM反加密系统传输作品，涵盖工业EBM、暗迪斯科、rave、darkwave、合成器朋克及后俱乐部实验等多种声音。以Brood Faye的《I Could B U》为例，作品将模拟合成器压力、恐怖朋克咬合感与工业金属碰撞混合，声乐在稀疏闪光中断续呈现，让节奏如同一场抽搐、诱惑与神秘仪式的复合体。整张合辑试图用身体性的失序与噪音回应技术的完美统治，将不完美的肉身痕迹作为对抗机器效率的核心武器。

items.body:
The jittery pulses and waking dream-like atmospheres of Dx2ov land on London’s Blank Mind for an album strafing between cut-up sound poetry and whisked garage-house.

“Dx2ov arrives on Blank Mind with Tonegues, his second vinyl LP following on from Interzona on Gost Zvuk in 2024. The LP title is a wordplay on the idea of speaking in tongues and sonic tonalities, echoing the process and dialogue that went into creating the record. Taken from a vast archive of material from 2019-2025, these ideas were arranged with the collaboration of label owner Sam Purcell and then completed with the long-distance assistance of Toupaz.

Tonegues is best seen through the lens of a beat-tape, with the playful flow and variety that the format provides, bursting with oddball ideas and punctuated with intangible vocal samples. Much like the LP’s beguiling, hand-drawn artwork by Wolfgang Matuschek, it is a glimpse into an inner world, a portal to somewhere uncanny and strange borne through imagination.

Light dub flourishes mix with footwork/IDM hybrids and understated, melancholic synthesis on ‘2018’, whilst the loose, rhythmic march of ‘Fon32’ evokes the dusty beatdown styles of early 2000s Detroit downtempo records. Whilst on one of the LP highlights ‘Trout’ he lays down a gleefully strange bed for the surrealist storytelling of Jacob Dwyer about interactions with dogs, dripping old houses and a perennial wish for the phone to ring with a heavy dub poetry slant. Dx2ov swiftly moves through more footwork adjacent, almost bedroom hyper-pop territories with a penchant for gabber kicks on ‘No Strings (feat DJ Paprika)’ and the maximalism of album closer 'Demetch' which continues in the tradition of wonky, mid-2010s UK bass music flips. The outcome is a confounding, unorthodox piece of work, zigzagging between forms, textures and moods.”

items._cn_summary: 这是Dx2ov的第二张黑胶专辑，收录于伦敦独立厂牌Blank Mind。创作素材来自2019至2025年间积累的大量素材，由厂牌主理人Sam Purcell协助编排，并经Toupaz远程合作完成。整张专辑以beat-tape的形式呈现，节奏松散自由，碎片化的语音采样与拼贴式声音诗歌贯穿始终。在风格上横跨dub氛围、footwork节奏实验、IDM合成器拼贴与车库律动，不拘泥于固定形态。'Trout'一曲以荒诞叙事配合dub诗歌念白，'No Strings'引入gabber踢鼓元素，末曲'Demetch'延续了2010年代中期英国bass音乐的扭曲美学。手绘封面与音乐共同构建出一个奇异而私密的内在世界。

items.body:
DJ Plead and rRoxymore with a sick debut collab of rhythmelodically restless productions, infusing limber, freewheeling styles with subtly psychedelic balearic melodics - a big one for followers of CCL, Batu, Nick León, Olof Dreijer, Joe, Nídia & Valentina Magaletti.

After meeting for the first time in 2019, Hermione Frank and Jarred Beeler got together at Frank's Berlin studio, slowly sculpting fractal geometries before finally adding the finishing spit and polish at Beeler's parents’ house in Sydney. Marking some of the first original material from either in a minute, the EP knits the duo’s rhythmic fascinations in three ways. 

‘Celestial’ splices a rolling 4/4 with quicksilver polyrhythms and zippy melodic motifs swept into hand-clap trills, imagining something like Olof Dreijer re-shaping Joe’s angular syncopations. ‘Read Wrong’ follows to foreground a thumb piano on a more pendulous, sub-weighted flex, inflected with DJ Plead’s signature palette of drum sounds and canny orchestral flashes at the right moments, dipping like D1’s more melodic works or that forthcoming Nídia & Valentina Magaletti pearl. 

The duo save their most hard-hitting for last, sliding speedy, dembow-inspired geometries through green-tinted clouds of electronics on a UKF-compatible offbeat threaded with swooping subs and flighty flutes. The momentum never lets up, but the two producers manage to evoke a mood that's as suited to a late-nite solo thing as it is to peak time wreckage. In other words; deceptively effortless gear that hits harder the louder it gets.

items.body: It was only a matter of time. In the cosmology of our music, one thing was certain: the orbits of Thelonious Monk and [Ahmed] were destined to overlap, after having crossed in the name of Ahmed Abdul-Malik, Monk's bassist in the late 1950s quartet, heard on 1958's Thelonious in Action and Misterioso , as well as on the album with John Coltrane at Carnegie Hall unearthed in 2005. Pat Thomas (piano), Seymour Wright (alto sax), Joel Grip (double bass), and Antonin Gerbal (drums) "make music about (Note: bear in mind this "about" because is the key to almost everything) Ahmed Abdul-Malik, they excavate, re-inhabit, and use a-new the now overlooked documents and fragmentary plans of his mid-20th-century synthetic vision to produce a new jazz imagination for the 21st century. [Ahmed] and Abdul share a critical engagement with time, specifically in challenging its linear trajectory and offering sites and modes of synthesis and rupture instead. In their music, fragments of time are scattered and re-arranged in the present". So says the band's official statement, which theoretically should explain everything. Theoretically. Malik (1927-1993), son of Caribbean immigrants, was a NYC bassist, oudist, composer, educator and philosopher, he played with Art Blakey, Earl Hines and Randy Weston and his albums Sahara (1958) and East Meets West (1960) fused aspects of Arabic and East African musics and thought, his committed long-term relationship with Sufi Islam and then-modern jazz and thinking, in revolutionary and vital way. But, as well as honoring these traditions, Malik's straddling, synthetic and inclusive vision is one of the great projects of imagination in jazz. He mixed sounds and ethics, meanings and beliefs in open, experimental ways, without any dogma and this became the true north for [Ahmed]: to visit and re-think his compositions and the process potential in them. This is why we emphasized the adverb "about": neither covers, nor lab experiments in cold musical eugenics; neither free jazz, nor classic (even two super skilled listeners and reviewers like Lee and Fotis, in past reviews, scratched their heads between amazement and ecstasy) but a hypnotic Black Monolith that has cast an enigmatic and fascinating shadow for some years, writing a new chapter destined to remain in the Annals of Music. From the very first time we heard them, the immediate reference for us, rather than the music, was the cubist painting, in which we found all the elements expressed by [Ahmed] and vice versa: the break with traditional perspective; the geometric decomposition; the simultaneity of views; the reduced color palette and the use of collage. Art must not portray reality but interpret it, like a cognitive tool, as per cubists’ First Commandment, and Pat Thomas & co. are exactly abiding by that. After 6 albums, (all excellent but “Giant Beauty” and “[Sama’a] (Audition)” are two real, unmissable, t-rex carnivorous records) and a 7-inch, here finally, after having engaged with Monk’s standards in various individual or collective ways, the hesitation is broken and [Ahmed] “Play Monk”: when a title says it all. In 2 CDs recorded in March 2025 at Fish Factory Studios (the same “Sama’a” recording sessions), with a cover photo of the legendary pianist at Fisherman’s Wharf in San Francisco, portrayed by the lens of Baroness Pannonica de Koenigswarter that alone is worth the purchase of the album, 6 standards (“Bye-Ya/Epistrophy,” “Friday Thirteenth,” “Round Midnight,” “Epistrophy,” “Evidence,” “Oskar T.)” are atomized in the particle accelerator, “transforming each composition into a shifting quantum time artifact. The melodic, harmonic, rhythmic, and spatial gestures of each piece become complex vernacular forms, creating a dialogue in time and a (red)shifting lens through which to view our material present. Into the fissures of Monk’s form, [Ahmed] pour their own play, colliding and dancing with Duke Ellington, Cecil Taylor, Caribbean diasporic music, European improvisation, and Jah Shaka in their pursuit of future music,” to borrow Otoroku’s notes. Too much? If you trust just a little bit in your humble writer: NOT.AT.ALL. As usual, they set out and ride pedal to metal, no self-indulgence or self-referential (or falsely free-form) rotating solos, but a “wall of sound” that Phil Spector would have liked to produce, where more than playing the notes, they use them and the ideas in and about them, as a vehicle for their unique imagination, moving from what they know into new uncharted, creative lands. It’s too easy to predict that this album will take no prisoners in our end-of-year Top Tens, but it’s even really hard to imagine what other albums will live up to it. We’d like to close with the words of the great Luke Stewart, certainly much more titled than us, in expressing a reflection on Abdul-Malik and [Amed]: “The journey of self-discovery, communing with the eternal sound. A musician steeped in multiple worlds; oceans apart yet closely connected in ancestral memory. Musicians such Abdul-Malik were able to experience the global community of sound warriors, drawing inspiration from ancient cultures to support personal investigation. The connection was made clear, the music of Africa would certainly influence the African in America despite the atrocities of the Middle Passage, chattel slavery and continued racist violence that sought to sever any connection to the continent. The beauty of Malik’s investigation is this original fusion of new music (Jazz) of the African in America with ancient music of Africa. It is a shining example of collaboration in culture, where the music is allowed to shine for itself. This is the inspiration that is being tapped, being explored in this collaboration where rhythm is the basis for the sound. Just like Malik, [Ahmed] allow the spirit of the collective push the sound as the music develops into exalted chaos. Joy Be Upon Us!”I Play Monk by أحمد [Ahmed] Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这支伦敦乐队以1950年代末曾与Thelonious Monk合作的低音提琴手兼哲学家Ahmed Abdul-Malik为创作出发点，对其融合阿拉伯与东非音乐元素、结合苏菲伊斯兰思想与现代爵士的"综合性愿景"进行深度挖掘与重新诠释。乐队以钢琴、阿尔托萨克斯、低音提琴和鼓的经典编制，对Malik的作曲材料进行解构、重组与再激活，在时间的线性轨迹上制造断裂与综合。乐评将其与立体派绘画相类比——打破传统透视、几何分解、多视角同时呈现、拼贴手法——强调这既非翻奏也非冷僻的实验，而是在Malik开创的融合伦理基础上，书写爵士史上一个新篇章。乐队此前已发行六张专辑，乐评特别推荐《Giant Beauty》与《[Sama'a] (Audition)》两张为不可错过的作品。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — "Un druide est giboyeux lorsqu'il se prend pour un neutrino" is the opening track of the second album by the French quartet Pryapisme; unable to settle on a single genre, they play them all?simultaneously. Much like Naked City, yet distinct, given their French origins and strong symphonic leanings, they weave together a hybrid of electronica, hardcore, jazz, space rock, industrial, and, of course, progressive music.There is a touch of video game sound, and with it, electronic music and psychedelia, that fits perfectly into that highly elastic, cultivated subgenre comprising diverse influences; this makes for an intriguing prospect when seeing them live.It is pure Krautrock infused with classical piano, maintaining a captivating, infectious rhythm, whether in complex time signatures reminiscent of King Crimson or the progressive electronica style of John Digweed.Random Jean Vigo continues to blend electronica with classical and, later, distinctly rock influences; it's like Daft Punk turning into Rick Wakeman and then Metallica... all coming together in the end. Once again: you'd have to see that live!"La notion de chiralit� de spin..." kicks off with a free-jazz vibe, featuring a layering of saxophones and the yowling of the guest cat "La Belette," alongside a guitar that alternates between violence and a highly solemn keyboard. If you aren't familiar with this fabulous quartet, you should start listening with "Lesbian Bordello," as that one-minute-forty-eight-second track rounds out the picture. "J'ai envie de te claquer" plays like a horror-tinged Nouvelle Vague parody, making even Frank Zappa look tame, while the genre-hopping continues, shifting from funk to TV themes as if channel-surfing... but on the radio.When they play jazz, as in Cochenille, membrane et volcanologie, they make it gritty and street-style, like something out of a film noir or the way John Zorn used to play back when he still played the sax, but then, atonal keyboard notes combined with percussion create a truly spellbinding kind of fugue, turning this entire contemporary blend into a genre unto itself."Jon-bon-jon-boutros-boutros-boutros-bovi-miou-miou" is worth it for the title alone... but it also features music with a deep, deep keyboard, so deep it takes on an Eastern progressive vibe, to the point where it sounds like Ryuichi Sakamoto is behind the keys, experimenting all over again."Je suis venu, j'ai vu, j'ai sagouinu" is a progressive hardcore funk track featuring numerous complex cuts and breaks, as well as jazzy trio-style digressions and explosive bursts of energy that blow the song, and the �lbum, wide open; indeed, when the piano is left playing solo, it sounds as sophisticated as Zappa during the Hot Rats era."La nuit sur le Mont-Chauvelu" sounds like a heavy metal orchestra doubling as a classical choir, incorporating fragments of classic horror themes, such as Mussorgsky's Night on Bald Mountain. It truly demonstrates their ability to go classical and epic, while also reimagining the material across genres ranging from heavy metal to jazz and Stevie Wonder-esque funk. The guitar work is serious, and throughout the album, the rhythm holds steady as the listener keeps pace with a musical carousel that promises plenty more spins, as many as a cat makes before settling down to sleep.

items.body: Miracle The Living Likeness of My Electric Daemon Relapse While The Living Likeness of My Electric Daemon is only the third LP from synthpop duo Miracle, its component members have certainly been busy with solo endeavours, soundtracking work and instrumental and production contributions in the eight years since their last record. Like all their work together, the classy, lushly produced sound of the record is supported by a strong central lyrical and thematic framework, adding additional depth to the listening experience. Broadly, the record revolves around the interaction of the spiritual and the physical world, invoking Christian theological doctrine and contemporary technology from Classicism to the cult of the smartphone. It’s heady and often esoteric stuff, but a fine match for the thoughtful, weighty approach to electronic music favoured by Steve Moore and Daniel O’Sullivan. Importantly, the music is never tied so closely to its big ideas that the songs become inaccessible; “Consolamentum Day” invokes the annihilation of the Cathars during the Crusades as a “recurring psychic event”, but you don’t need to unravel or even acknowledge its central metaphor to enjoy the warm synth chords, peppy melody or O’Sullivan’s evocative vocals, delivered in Latin or English. Similarly, opener “Ambrosia” is thick with gnostic reference (O’Sullivan sweetly singing “Caduceus ascеnds to axis mundi” is both bizarre and somehow compelling), with the music taking on an even more reverential tone, even in its funky disco guitar accents and analogue and digital synth textures. And really, whether or not you can make heads or tails of what these songs are about without opening multiple Wikipedia tabs, they’re so lovely its hard not to be drawn into them. “The Eye” has a pleasantly understated melody that plays off its bubbling synth bass, the vocals smoothly gliding across its sequences as they slowly resolve into its baroque climax. “Fluid Window” brings in guest vocalist Rose Keeler-Schaffeler for a slowburning, twinkling ballad that splits the tonal difference between reverence and sensuality, a relaxed ecstasy in its exploration of the digital world. When Miracle pull out the stops on the maximal synthwave of “Time is the Fire” (“in which we burn”, natch) it’s positively elating, the relative simplicity of its clarion lead and kick snare drums bringing an inspirational vibe to its fatalistic view of history. The Living Likeness of My Electric Daemon is a rare beast indeed, lavish and full of import in its design and production, and arcane and even impenetrable in its subject matter. And yet, those two facets reinforce one another rather than contrast, the richness of its sonics infusing the lyrics with meaning and weight. Miracle have built a grandiose modern synthpop record, as potent and as mystifying as it is mysterious, bless them. Recommended. Buy it. The Living Likeness Of My Electric Daemon by Miracle The post Miracle, “The Living Likeness of My Electric Daemon” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 这是合成器流行二人组 Miracle 的第三张全长专辑，围绕灵性与物质世界的互动展开，借用基督教神学教义与当代科技意象构建主题框架。文本涉及卡特里派消亡等历史隐喻，并混入诺斯底主义符号，使歌词充满学术化的密语感。制作上以模拟与数字合成器织体为核心，辅以迪斯科吉他切分与巴洛克式编排，嘉宾人声在抒情曲目中带来缓慢燃烧的张力。乐队成员将过往独奏、配乐与制作经验注入此作，使整体制作层次丰富且氛围浓郁。主题的晦涩与音色的温暖形成相互支撑——歌词的重量感被配器的丰盈托住，听者无需解读所有典故仍能感受到音乐本身的吸引力。专辑在神圣与感性之间游走，兼具神秘主义气质与流行可听性。

items.body:
Edgar puts his kinky, Latinate stamp on myriad styles of Hi-NRG, gothic synth-pop, and cumbia, including a cover of Amanda Lear’s ‘Follow Me’ among its bevy of sleazy darkroom snax...

"Edgar debuts on Dark Entries with Pavor, an 11 track LP of sleazy disco, warped synthpop, and gothic cumbia. Veteran musician Luis Gutierrez has spent the past two decades touring in bands, running Lalalandia Studio, and building his practice in Oakland and Guadalajara. But now, for his first solo outing, he has become Edgar, a pop star who knows no limits! “Edgar feels mightier than anyone but is always reduced to his vices” says Gutierrez, and Pavor delivers vices in spades.

From the opening salvos of “Otra Agua,” it’s clear we’re in for a wild ride: seasick synths slide along slamming disco beats, menacingly chanted vocals sit amid a flurry of careening horror movie samples. The mischief does not abate as we’re guided through a demented funhouse of genre detournements. Edgar puts his indelible fingerprints over every inch of this vinyl, from uptempo numbers like the spooky chip-tune frenzy of “Nunca Mas” to the twisted cumbia of “Panteon.” We’re even treated to a fairly faithful (and majestic) Spanish-language cover of Amanda Lear’s “Follow Me,” here titled “Sigueme.” EBM, space disco, and horror movie soundtracks all find their way into the mix on Pavor, but the diverse palette comes together perfectly, like a Yello album for the 21st century.

On Pavor, Edgar brings us a healthy dose of pure excess, reminding us that dread can be a hell of a lot of fun. "
items._cn_summary: Edgar 首张专辑《Pavor》由资深音乐人 Luis Gutierrez 呈现，融合了 Hi-NRG、哥特合成器流行、EBM、太空迪斯科与恐怖电影配乐等多种风格，并加入扭曲的昆比亚节奏。专辑由 Dark Entries 厂牌发行，包含对 Amanda Lear 的西班牙语翻唱曲目。制作上将疾速的迪斯科节拍、不安的合成器旋律、阴森的人声吟诵与电影采样并置，形成一种怪诞的游乐园式氛围。评论将其比作21世纪的 Yello 专辑，凸显其在类型混合上的大胆与连贯性。这种将拉丁音乐传统与欧洲暗潮电子语汇并置的手法，为专辑带来了独特的文化张力与实验趣味。

items.body:
Squid guitarist Anton Pearson takes a deep dive into kosmische waters on his solo debut, stacking elongated guitar drones, synth textures and organ vamps into billowing, free-flowing long form compositions.

It's pretty obvious how this one came about - the title gives it away immediately. While Pearson was touring incessantly with Warp-signed post-punk outfit Squid, his mind wandered incessantly, dreaming of a sound that Squid couldn't match up to. It haunted him, in fact, until he was back in his Brighton studio and able to experiment with the tools that surrounded him, not just guitars but synths and vintage keyboards. Thinking about the hallucinatory touring experience, music began to materialise that felt just as surreal, mundane and faintly entrancing. And it's a feeling that's best represented on the epic side-long opener, 'Driving Past the Muscular Cows in Belgium'. A good half of the duration is spent fixating on a restless drone that fidgets and buzzes like a car engine, retreating occasionally when Pearson's guitar mimics oncoming traffic. And in the second half, the low-end rumble falls away and the track begins to lift itself to the clouds, fading in vanishing synth arpeggios that form a bewitching final act conclusion. It's unexpected stuff, more like early Emeralds than anything Squid have ever stamped their logo on.

After the Fennesz-like granulations of 'Builder in a Bottle', Pearson hits firmer landscape with 'Tintinnabulation I', the first of two bell studies that lend the album some conceptual weight. Pearson admits that his debut came about through studio experimentation, which can often result in sketchy ideas that don't quite hang together. But 'Driving...' plays like a single thought and the two 'Tintinnabulation' tracks shine a light on the sonic space Pearson was immersed in. The titular chimes come in various formulations, smeared into shrill waves at the beginning before they're echoed by tense electric and acoustic piano phrases. And on the second, seven-minute section, the chimes are subsumed by thick, syrupy drones that increase in density until we're left with a spectrum-filling wall of synthesised sound.

items._cn_summary: Squid乐队吉他手Anton Pearson首张个人专辑深入宇宙迷幻音乐领域，将绵延的吉他嗡鸣、合成器肌理与风琴段落堆叠成自由流动的长篇作品。专辑灵感源于他在巡演途中对无法在乐队中实现的声音的执念，回到布莱顿工作室后通过吉他、合成器与复古键盘进行实验，试图捕捉那种超现实、琐碎又略带催眠感的旅途体验。开篇曲以近半小时的篇幅铺展不安分的嗡鸣底色，模拟引擎震动与车流声，随后低频退去，合成器琶音如薄雾般升腾收束。后续曲目以钟声研究为核心概念，将铃声揉入尖锐声波，与紧张的电钢琴与原声钢琴交织，后半段被浓稠的嗡鸣吞没，形成密集的合成器音墙。整体呈现出从具象声响到抽象声谱空间的渐变逻辑。

Recorded in 1991, 'Rise' sweeps up all known recorded material from A.R. Kane's Rudy Tambala and Cranes vocalist Alison Shaw, aka inrain, compiling a classic 7” for Rough Trade with additional, previously unreleased tracks. It’ll no doubt provide many with a first introduction to a prescient project by two scene legends, delving into shoegaze, dub, electro and trip-hop refractions of the highest order. It's the most essential Music From Memory release in a hot minute, crucial listening for all A.R Kane obsessives (that should be all of you) or anyone into Seefeel, Locust, Zurich.

For someone for whom Cranes' ‘Tomorrow's Tears’ and A.R Kane’s ‘Lolita’ are two absolute foundational texts, this reissue is basically something like a holy grail. Back in 1991, inrain appeared on Rough Trade's Singles Club series with a brief but brilliant 7" that sounded as if it'd been beamed in from another planet. A.R. Kane had already broken the mold, but these three tracks juxtaposed Shaw's dreamy vocals with dubby, spacious electronics and shimmering guitars in a way that wouldn't really rise to prominence until years later. Music From Memory do the heavy lifting here, remastering that original 7" from the original DAT tapes and adding the extra track 'Biology' and an alternate version of 'Sleep' to bump up the package. 

It's those original tracks that have us by the throat - we really can't believe they've been so slept on over the years. '...And Julie Rose' sounds like it should have been picked up for a Duophonic release a decade later, while 'Sleep' completely pre-empts Seefeel's 'More Like Space EP' that wouldn't appear for another couple of years. 

Prophetic, brilliant stuff.
items._cn_summary: 1991年录制的这张专辑由A.R. Kane的Rudy Tambala与Cranes主唱Alison Shaw合作完成，原始三首作品曾在Rough Trade单曲俱乐部发行，2023年由Music From Memory厂牌从原始DAT母带重新母带处理并扩充曲目。音乐将Shaw空灵飘渺的人声与dub质感、电子律动和闪烁的吉他层叠融合，呈现出超越时代的声音面貌。评论指出其声音预言了Seefeel后来的空间感探索以及Duophonic厂牌的美学走向。专辑横跨shoegaze、dub、electro和trip-hop多种风格，编曲疏密有致，氛围营造极具沉浸感，是英国地下音乐史上被严重低估的实验性合作项目。

items.body:
Mannequin tap an arsenal of secret German electro weapons, as played by Helena Hauff and I-F, hailing a pivotal era when body music set the scene for electroclash, stuffed with zingers FFO Le Syndicat Electronique, I-F, Dopplereffekt, Drexciya, Legowelt, Adult., The Hacker, DMX Krew, Gesloten Cirkel, and early Bunker Records electro 

“Active around the turn of the millennium, both projects share the involvement of producer Ive Müller while developing distinct collaborations and approaches to electronic music. H.E.I.M. Elektronik was founded in 1996 by Holger Erlenwein and Ive Müller (after the two artists split in 1999, Müller continued using the name), while MAS 2008 is the project of Ive Müller together with René Kirchner. Though separate entities, the two projects explored a similar sonic territory: stripped-down electro, minimal electronics and machine-driven body music shaped by analog hardware and a raw DIY production ethos.

The roots of Müller’s work go back to the final years of the DDR. As a teenager he worked as a licensed DJ — officially known as a “Schallplattenunterhalter” — operating a travelling disco across Saxony. With limited access to official Western releases, music circulated through cassette recordings taped from West German radio stations such as RIAS Berlin, NDR2 and Bayern3. Together with friends he travelled between youth clubs and discos around Leipzig with a “rolling discotheque”: a Russian Wolga pulling a trailer loaded with Electro-Voice sound systems sourced through the black market.

At the turn of the 2000s this background in underground electronic culture resurfaced in a series of recordings rooted in electro, EBM and minimal machine music. The tracks collected on Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 capture this moment: cold sequences, driving rhythms and stark synthetic textures produced with a direct and uncompromising approach.

Compiled and remastered by Rude 66 from the original sources, Electronic Corporation 2000–2002 documents a small but fascinating chapter of German underground electronics from the early digital era.”
items._cn_summary: Mannequin厂牌将两支德国电子项目H.E.I.M. Elektronik与MAS 2008的作品合辑发行，由Rude 66从原始素材重新混音并母带处理。制作人Ive Müller自1990年代末起活跃于德国地下电子场景，早年在东德时期以青少年DJ身份运营流动迪斯科，录音素材来自西德广播电台的磁带翻录。专辑聚焦2000至2002年的创作阶段，以模拟硬件为核心，强调直接而不妥协的制作态度。声音呈现冷峻的序列线条、驱动型节奏与裸露的合成器纹理，根植于electro、EBM与极简机械音乐的传统脉络。与Le Syndicat Electronique、Drexciya、Legowelt、Dopplereffekt等地下electro场景共享美学谱系，延续Bunker Records时期的硬核电声探索。整体呈现一段德国地下电子历史的微型切片，DIY精神与冷战末期文化背景交织于其中。

items.body:
Modular bod M. Geddes Gengras gets the band back together on 'Guestlist', roping in an estimable team of collaborators (including Christina Carter, WANDA GROUP, Greg Fox, Ben Chasny and Meg Duffy, among others) to recapture the lightning in a bottle energy of Chicago's early post-rock era, when sounds would criss-cross over each other relatively freely.

Despite technology being accessible, commonplace even, it's still relatively difficult to find the sweet spot between live instrumentation and electronics. Modular synthesis, that thrives on its self-contained, often unpredictable moments of serendipity, adds an even more problematic element. You can make it work, sure, but so much of what we like about modular music is that it doesn't feel as if it's been looped into structures that file down its sharp edges. Gengras sets himself a challenge here, working like a synthesist but also drawing on his experience playing in bands - he sees both sides, which gives him a head-start. And he's also got the good sense to think back to an era where the possibilities felt endless: the "early Pro Tools" era as James Toth writes in the accompanying notes, when bands like Tortoise and The Sea and Cake were looking at artists like Autechre and AFX and wondering what techniques they could integrate.

And 'Guest List' is undoubtedly Gengras' most ambitious record to date. There's more to it than personnel, too - proper songs, a far cry from the hazy new age-tinted synth jams that we heard on 'Expressed, I Noticed Silence' or the post-kosmische "ROMpler worship" of 'QUIK-MELT', appear in the dense tangle of instruments and expressions. While the 11-minute 'The List is Millions Long' initially seems to not-so-subtly reference Tortoise's 'Millions Now Living...' with its chiming guitars and motorik beat (supplied by Portland-based sound artist Colin Blanton, no less), it gets more complicated when Will Epstein's saxophone enters the frame. And that harmonic complexity remains when the track melts into 'Laplace/Montagne' and Gengras' synth belches are augmented by Chasny's golden shreds. Hell, there are even vocals on 'Seven Dials' provided by Austin's Cory Plump, who shouts listlessly over Gengras' sunny arpeggios, Fox's drums and Duffy's riffs.

Prepare yourself, 'Guest List' is not the M. Geddes Gengras you're likely to be expecting. There's even a spoken word intro to the album's brilliant finale '"The Weather"' from cult social media star and sometime genius WANDA GROUP. Proper good.
items._genre: experimental electronic / post-rock / synth / krautrock-influenced / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这是一张以模块化合成器为骨架、召集众多乐手合作的概念专辑，核心探索在于如何在电子编程与即兴现场演奏之间找到平衡点。制作人借鉴芝加哥后摇滚黄金年代的创作思路——那种声音自由交叠、乐队结构松散却充满化学反应的状态，试图在当代语境下重建类似Tortoise和The Sea and Cake时期的质感。专辑中既有11分钟的长篇器乐作品，将循环摩托节奏、合成器低鸣、萨克斯和吉他即兴层叠缠绕，也有人声和口语朗诵段落，打破纯器乐框架。整体编排密度较高，乐手之间形成复杂的和声对话，是一次对模块化音乐结构化表达的有意义尝试。

items.body:
If you thought Dave Huismans’ (aka 2562, aka A Made Up Sound) recent return as ex_libris was good, his new, long-form minimalist dub special for Fergus Jones’ FELT label under the "In Transit" alias is another leap up, giving wings to nearly 40 mins of the finest shine-eyed downbeat pressure this side of NWAQ/154, Studio Pankow, Civilistjävel! or Rod Modell - proper top tier business.

In Transit sees Huismans go one step deeper down the rabbit hole he entered as ex_libris a few months ago. Like that project, it finally sees light of day after many years marinading in folders he would return to irregularly as a sort of meditative practice, dusting down loops and seeing how they connected after some dozen years hidden away in the archive.

When he finally got to unravelling them, they revealed a vibe that’s a far cry from his earliest work, and although sharing a slower, hazier aesthetic with ex_libris, he would logically push that sound deep into a sort of subconscious hypnagogia guided by sixth senses and shorn of any urgent, rhythmic impulses. The result is hugely absorbing  - deep without losing momentum, winding down different paths that feel engaging rather than forgettable.

At a rested heart rate the tracks swim on the imagination from distant, sonorous clanks and whispered chords in ‘A.33’, thru the tongue-tip thizz and searching tendrils of ‘A.2829’, to the subaquatic jazz sway of ‘A.18’, gently surfacing for air in the blissed iridescence of an ‘A.25’ shades away from NWAQ’s ‘Dead Bears’ vibes shared with the crystalline synth motifs of ‘A.19’, and vaporised to exquisite effect in ‘A.3132.’  

Special one.
items._cn_summary: Dave Huismans 以 In Transit 化名推出的这张全长专辑，源自他在档案中封存十余年的循环素材，经过长期沉淀后重新拆解重组。作品延续了他近年 ex_libris 项目的缓慢朦胧美学，但更进一步剥离了节奏驱动力，进入一种近乎睡眠边缘的潜意识状态。整张专辑近四十分钟，没有紧迫的律动脉冲，而是以低频嗡鸣、水下般的爵士律动、远处金属敲击和晶体合成器音色缓缓铺陈。曲目之间形成连续的声学旅程，从低沉回响到水晶般的旋律碎片，从朦胧漂浮到精妙的蒸发消散，层层递进却不失内在凝聚力。作品与 NWAQ、Civilistjävel! 等当代极简氛围制作共享美学谱系，展现了创作者在长期封存中重新发现声音连结的冥想式实践。

items.body:
Working his hi-BPM (bull)rushes into swampy environmental recordings, Richie Culver returns to Boro's Industrial Coast with his most impressionistic and substantial Quiet Husband set so far, short-circuiting distinctions between his visual and aural practices with keenly synaesthetic nous hugely advised to admirers of W92’s Omen Wapta, aspects of Chain Reaction’s Matrix, or even H-Fusion’s ‘Captured Entities’.

‘The Architecture of Perception’ examines the lived and structural correspondences between techno and painting, proposing that tracks in the club function as colours do in the studio. On 'Composition', Culver sketches out his rough blueprint; first playing rich, noisy nighttime sounds - chirping crickets, oozing liquids - before looping them behind knee-trembling 185BPM kicks and metallic clangs. It's music that seems to revel in its own contradictory nature: minimal maximalism; faster, grubbier and more provocative than you'd ever expect to hear in a club.

'Abstraction' dispenses with the rhythm altogether, concentrating on creeping and evocative jungle ambiance that lubricates the brain for 'Duration’, where Culver's concept snaps into gear with buzzing cybernetic calls and sonorous outdoor sounds that dissolve into undulating 4/4 thuds. It'd be daft to label it dub techno, but if you compare Culver's muckiest gear to Basic Channel's earliest, most saturated mixing desk experiments, there's a similar level of intentionality: an understanding of space and tonal colour that permeates the rippling drive of the music. And Culver never lets his breakneck dancefloor instincts take precedence over his blustery experiments. The momentum flips back and forth, darting from the dancefloor to the bathrooms to the darkroom, heading outside for a lungful of fresh air (or a cig) before taking an about turn and rummaging thru it all again.
items._genre: experimental techno / industrial / dub techno / field recording
items._cn_summary: Richie Culver 的 Quiet Husband 系列推出新作，将高 BPM 节奏与沼泽般的环境录音相融合，打通视觉与听觉实践的边界。专辑探讨俱乐部音乐与绘画的结构对应关系，把音色当作色彩来调度。《Composition》以夜间田野声景打底，叠入 185 BPM 的金属撞击与失真低频；《Abstraction》完全抛弃节拍，转向丛林氛围；《Duration》则以赛博蜂鸣与户外采样过渡到 4/4 脉动。整体在极简与极繁之间反复切换，从舞池到暗室再到户外穿梭不停，呈现出对空间与色调的有意经营，速度与粗糙质感并存，与 Basic Channel 早期的饱和混音实验遥相呼应。

items.body:
An advanced masterclass in Berlin beat science, ‘Wireless’ is the final and arguably strongest solo release by T++; aka Torsten Pröfrock, an artist with a long lineage of important releases under numrous aliases - Dynamo, Erosion,Log, Resilent, Traktor, Various Artists and more - a true pillar of Berlin's Techno legacy.

First issued by Honest Jon’s in 2010, the 2x12” features samples of singer and ndingidi-player Ssekinomu (originally found on the EMI archival dive ‘Bellyachers, Listen - Songs From East Africa, 1938-46’) reworked by Pröfrock into a volley of rambunctious but rudely disciplined club workouts some 75 years later. In many other hands, this could have been just another passable cut ’n splice edit, but T++ treats the material with a balance of reverence and raving license, highlighting an instinctive understanding of the original music's intent and purpose, and their deep rooted connection to modern fast rap and hardcore dance musics.

The four tracks amount to a contemporary classic in their field and also exist in a strong tradition of German artists ranging from Stockhausen to Can and Basic Channel whose music has crucially incorporated the fluid, rolling nature and spectra of African drumming patterns. However, it’s vital to point out that T++’s take on African drumming is also filtered thru a love of UK music - Jungle, D&B, garage, dubstep - meaning that his rhythms are properly underlined with syncopated, technoid basslines owing as much to Kingston, Jamaica as Brixton and Sheffield in the UK.

For anyone who had been intently listening to Pröfrock's output since his Traktor gems, thru his Dynamo aces, to early work with Monolake and his string of seminal T++ 12”s in the 2000’s, on its release in 2010 ‘Wireless’ quickly came to epitomise his approach to broken techno production at its most open-ended and inexorable. Between the itchy, sprung step of ‘Cropped’, the puckish darkside torque of ‘Anyi’, a voodoo communal in ‘Voice No Bodies’, and the reanimated spirits of ‘Dig’ you have some of the finest mutant techno ever cut to vinyl.

An absolute must-have for dancers and DJs.
items._genre: techno / broken beat / experimental electronic / dub techno
items._cn_summary: T++（Torsten Pröfrock）作为柏林电子音乐场景的重要人物，其专辑《Wireless》将1938至1946年东非歌手与恩丁迪琴演奏者Ssekinomu的档案录音素材重新解构，融入碎拍techno框架。乐评指出该作品在节奏处理上实现了非洲鼓乐传统与柏林硬核舞曲美学的深度融合，同时受到英国Jungle、D&B、Garage、Dubstep等音乐的影响，低频线条兼具牙买加金斯敦式的律动与英国城市场景的techno质感。四首曲目分别呈现出跳跃步态、暗潮扭矩、巫毒社群感以及重生的灵性意象，被视为mutant techno领域的典范之作。发行厂牌Honest Jon's以深度挖掘全球档案音乐闻名，强化了这张专辑在文化语境上的跨时空对话意义。整体呈现出对原始素材的尊重与锐舞释放之间的精妙平衡，是电子音乐与世界音乐融合的一次重要实践。

items.body:
A rare window into Angolan musical culture. Guitarist Mário Rui Silva folds traditional Angolan and West African rhythms into European jazz forms, creating music that's subtle, beautiful and completely distinct. 

'Stories from Another Time' compiles music from three of Silva's 1980s albums, "Sung’Ali", "Tunapenda Afrika" and "Koizas dum Outru Tempu". Silva was a researcher and intellectual who was motivated to find the roots of Angolan culture in spite of its centuries-long struggle with colonization. Spurred on by Angolan musical legend Liceu Vieira Dias of traditional band Ngola Ritmos, Silva wanted to understand the politics and spiritualism behind Angolan music. Dias took traditional semba and kazukuta rhythms and infused them into contemporary music in the '40s and '50s, helping Angola to find national pride as the country struggled to assert itself after years of colonial rule.

Luanda-born Silva attempted to do similar with his music - and while it sounds aesthetically similar to Brazilian music of the 1970s, this was almost accidental. Silva was in fact attempting to move away from Portugese-centered culture and its tropical fetishism, and develop a sound that was purely Angolan. The music is hard to place, it sounds almost out of time, both ancient and surprisingly contemporary, with soft pop hooks underpinned by complex polyrhythms and chiming mbira. The fusion feels fluid and considered - there's no cynicism here at all, rather Silva approaches his sounds with a deft, open-hearted charm that rings from every word and lightly-picked note. Huge recommendation.
items._genre: Angolan jazz / world fusion / afro-jazz / ethno-jazz / traditional polyrhythm
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了安哥拉吉他手Mário Rui Silva在1980年代发行的三张专辑，追溯他将安哥拉传统semba与kazukuta节奏融入欧洲爵士形式的探索。作为研究者的Silva受安哥拉音乐传奇Liceu Vieira Dias启发，试图摆脱葡萄牙殖民文化框架，建立纯粹属于安哥拉的独立音乐语言。他的创作融合了传统节奏与复杂多声部律动，加入清脆的mbira音色，呈现出既古老又具有当代感的听觉体验。虽然整体音色与1970年代巴西音乐有相似之处，但这并非有意模仿，而是源于相似的非洲根源。Silva的音乐以轻盈的拨奏和开放的编曲态度著称，融合手法流畅而深思熟虑，展现了去殖民化背景下安哥拉文化寻根的独特艺术视角。

items.body:
Ghost Dubs & The Bug duppy the latter’s cult, isolationist ambient excursion of 2022 with apposite measures of lead-boot trod and atmospheric levity for the hardest-to-please industrial dub freaks.

Selected cuts from ’Sub Zero’ - Kevin Richard Martin’s concerted return to interests in ambient-dub-noise fundamentals - are robustly togged out with bass insulation and Goretextured to the elements for a supremely crushing session that benefits from the biggest speakers you can lay yr mitts on. It catches KRM arguably in his imperial phase, sustaining a tear of substantial gear penned under his own name since ‘Sirens’ (Room 40, 2019) deep into the belly of his sound, to now clasp these chiral aspects of his steez - the supine, sunken, and strongback, stepping - in a deathly bind.

KMR’s key spar and Pressure MVP, Ghost Dubs goes super dank and wide on his half, opening subterranean caverns of space below ‘When I’m Gone’, punctuated only by abandoned ice-breaker clank and timber-shiver chorales, before pushing leagues below into knackered Porter Ricks or Rhythm & Sound terrain on rework of ‘Sorrow’. Martin keeps up his end of the bargain with a sonorous diffusion of ‘Screwed’, all icy plangency and keeling bass recalling aspects of Mika Vainio’s ‘Kilo’, then plumbing guttural crevasses of the spirit on remix of ‘Too Human’.
items._genre: ambient dub / industrial dub / noise / dark ambient
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Kevin Richard Martin 2022年个人专辑《Sub Zero》的混音再制版本，由The Bug和Ghost Dubs分别操刀。混音将原作的孤立主义氛围推向更沉重的工业dub领域，以厚重的低频绝缘和粗粝的噪声质感重新打造。Ghost Dubs的部分拓展了深邃的地下声场空间，融入冰船撞击金属的残响和木材震颤的和声，并下沉至Porter Ricks与Rhythm & Sound式的极简techno-dub地带。Kevin Richard Martin本人的混音则以冰冷的回响和沉稳的低频铺陈，唤起Mika Vainio式的极简氛围质感，并在更深处挖掘低频的裂隙。整张作品适合在大型音箱系统上播放，呈现出深沉、压迫、层次丰富的声学建筑，是工业dub与暗潮氛围融合的扎实之作。

items.body:
Topdown Dialectic’s solo debut bow on False Aralia rounds up over a decade of material in supremely elusive style & pattern - all rug-pulling rhythms and hallucinatory fractals wrapped up with proper, hyperreal frisson. Massive chef’s kiss FFO Vladislav Delay, Beatrice Dillon, Paperclip Minimiser, Purelink, Marc Leclair.

An artist keenly observed since initial gestures on /\\Aught in the early ‘10s, and throughout their cult LP trilogy for Peak Oil during 2018-2021; Topdown Dialectic has become a unique facet of C.21st dub electronics, adored for their grasp of diffused spatio-textural sorcery and wraithlike grooves. Anyone paying close attention to emergent sounds via Peak Oil and its False Aralia offshoot may have guessed at TD’s signature, watermarked imprint on the Borgesian Term EP of late ’25, which can now be confirmed as the work of one and the same Izaak Schlossmann; a photographer and producer patently in possession of heightened proprioceptions and a rewardingly patient approach to lushly dissociative sonification. In other words, he makes some of the sexiest electronic music out there - stuff that genuinely feels like it was made this century - and his latest practically leaves you kissing the sky thru its 80 minutes of lip-biting, skin tingling pressure. 

On 16 tracks timed at exactly 5 minutes each, we’re placed in the presence of suggestive sorcery, eliding unarchived material and jams in a unique ecology of oneiric physics. Never overtly showy or overblown, there’s nevertheless a staggering level of ingenuity and synaesthetic effect to its detailed construction and gaseous fractals resembling the LSD or DMT experience. The label themselves compare its nuance to “the flicker of a candle over a desk of drum machines in a Midwestern basement, or the “first blush of sunlight over a tiny campground as subwoofers creak in the distance”, which proves a perfectly poetic analog to its digitally-smudged refractions and tongue-tip spectral tumescence. 

Ultimately, it’s a singular pleasure to immerse the senses in Topdown Dialectic’s self-contained soundsphere, and never more substantially so than on ‘False LP A’. Longtime enthusiasts will surely recognise his skill in parsing salient aspects of Basic Channel x Rhythm & Sound, and their descendants in Vladislav Delay or Pole, reframing those templates in far more uncertain space with a real animist magick. Each work feels tangibly, ambiguously alive, breathing with dynamics and more voluminous, macro scales, and iridescent with voices and details that commands attentive listeners who will have a field day zoning in/out to its illusive, holographic projections and syncopated chronics.
